paras.text: Point-of-care testing (POCT) for disease detection and management is a highly practical and impactful approach, particularly in resource limited settings [1,2]. POCT can enable rapid linkage to care, effective response to disease outbreak and enhance healthcare efficiencies [2–5]. POCT requires minimal infrastructure, and it includes various modalities such as lateral flow assays, handheld devices, near-POC benchtop analyzers among other modalities [6–8]. National essential diagnostic lists (NEDL) in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC) include POC tests among priority in-vitro diagnostic tests crucial for the population’s health needs [9,10]. However, studies suggest that only 19% of the population in LMIC have access to the simplest POC tests for healthy pregnancy and non-communicable diseases (NCDs), excluding HIV and malaria tests [11].

Policymakers, implementers, and funders have largely overlooked POC diagnostics, while shortages of trained testing staff and unreliable supplies have further widened this diagnostic gap [5,12]. Closing the diagnostic gap for six tracer conditions (HIV, hypertension, diabetes mellitus (DM), syphilis, tuberculosis (TB), congenital hepatitis B) has been shown to potentially avert 1.1 million premature deaths in LMICs [11].

Patients typically seek care at primary health care (PHC) facilities, which often lack on-site laboratory services and rely on overburdened frontline healthcare workers (HCWs) for POCT [13]. In these settings, frontline HCW (nurses and clinical staff) often lack flexible time to perform POC tests for HIV, TB, cryptococcal meningitis, malaria, syphilis, hepatitis, cholera, diabetes mellitus among other tests.

Even though significant strides have been made, advancement toward achieving global milestone targets for elimination of AIDS, viral hepatitis, tuberculosis, NCDs (DM, hypertension), and other key health priorities (including syphilis, gonorrhea) remains insufficient and uneven in many regions [14–19]. This is largely due to persistent gaps in screening and diagnosis. With an ever-expanding range of POC tests available, current testing strategies largely reliant on frontline HCW, with limited task sharing to lay cadres [5], are increasingly insufficient. New approaches are needed, especially as national programs face unprecedented funding challenges [20], even while testing demands continue to rise.

WHO endorses task sharing (TS) for POCT with non-laboratory personnel [2,21] to address HCW shortages. TS involves rationally re-distributing tasks from professional HCWs to trained lay health workers (LHWs) [21] through collaboration. LHW are personnel who deliver healthcare-related services but do not possess formal professional or paraprofessional qualifications. Studies have shown that LHWs (counsellors, community health care workers, health diagnostic assistants, phlebotomists, health surveillance assistants) with adequate training can reliably perform POCT services [3,10,22–25]. Nevertheless, other studies note that decentralized TS for POCT demands support from national laboratories and programmes to ensure proper training, supervision and quality assurance [3,26]. Additional research indicates that the implementation of TS for POCT often faces practical hurdles stemming from lack of supportive national policy and funding strategies, intricate governance for POCT conducted outside laboratories and rigid regulations upholding professional task boundaries [5,10].

In 2011, Médecins Sans Frontières/Doctors without borders (MSF) partnered with the Malawi Ministry of Health to improve access to quality HIV/TB care services in Nsanje district, primarily through mentorship and targeted health system strengthening activities. Nsanje is a remote, largely rural district in southernmost Malawi and it is the second poorest district with 74.3% living in poverty [27–29]. Patients face challenges in accessing healthcare due to long distances to health facilities and the flood-prone environment together with socio-economic barriers and this leads to late presentation to care and poor retention. Clinical mentorship, supportive supervision and commodities for the implementation of the AHD package, including differentiated ART delivery models, were provided to Nsanje District Hospital (NDH) and seven other health centres (Sorgin, Kalemba, Phokera, Nyamithuthu, Tengani, Mbenje and Ndamera), in a phased manner as from 2018 [30].

The Malawi department of HIV/AIDS together with non-governmental organizations like Partners-in-Hope deployed health diagnostic assistants (HDAs) to health facilities, to support HIV and syphilis testing services including collection of blood samples for early infant diagnosis (EID), and HIV Viral load (HIV VL), among other roles [31]. HDAs are a lay cadre with a minimum education qualification of a high school certificate and trained for 4-weeks in HIV testing services. Over 1000 HDAs were seconded to over 500 health facilities across all districts of Malawi in year 2015 [32]. From this pre-existing cadre, MSF recruited and provided further training for 3 days on operational procedures for CD4 cell count testing using PIMA instrument (Abbott MA, USA; formerly Alere), urine Determine TB LAM test (Abbott MA, USA; formerly Alere) and IMMY CrAg lateral flow tests (IMMY Diagnostics, Norman, USA) as well as result documentation, device maintenance and quality control monitoring in POC testing. Training included theoretical and practical segments on sample collection, test performance, result interpretation, biosafety, and confidentiality; following a standardized package previously described [24,31]. Competency was assessed using structured checklists prior to deployment, with all LHWs passing before field deployment [24,25]. The LHWs were each deployed to MSF supported health facilities in Nsanje district and their role was to conduct testing for AHD as well as other POCT (HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, malaria). The LHWs also conducted other activities including collecting dry blood spot (DBS) samples for HIV viral load (VL) and HIV early infant diagnosis (EID). Ongoing performance evaluation and supportive supervision were regularly provided to LHWs by the MSF district laboratory manager, and this included monthly site audits, regular QC record review, annual competency re-assessment, proficiency testing, and troubleshooting support to ensure quality assurance (QA) in POCT. Testing consumables were supplied for POC tests.

At each PHC, a dedicated ‘POC room’ was set-up and equipped with POC tests as well as a PIMA CD4 device and it was often in direct proximity to the outpatient section to facilitate prompt results return. Patients eligible for testing were identified in the triage and sent to the POC room and thereafter returned to the consultation room for further clinical management. The objective was to return all testing results to the clinicians within 30–60 minutes from sample venesection to allow for quick diagnosis and further management decisions in the same clinical encounter. MSF clinical staff supported and mentored national clinical staff for same-day result review and patient management. Details of the intervention in PHCs can be found elsewhere [30].

paras.sec_title: AHD testing cascade for PHCs facilities in model 2
paras.text: Across all health facilities, the total PIMA CD4 error rate was 8.3% (70/840). The leading causes were invalid test error code 860 (36.8%), followed by error code 201 (18.7%) and error code 940 (12.9%), which together accounted for almost 70% of all errors. According to manufacturer recommendations, error code 860 typically stems from equipment or reagent-related issues whereas error codes 940 and 201 can be either operator or equipment-related [31].

Task-shifted POC testing was linked to a near-two-fold increase in the POC tests conducted in model 2 compared to model 1 as well as associated with a significantly increased proportion of samples referred to the district laboratory for molecular testing. By delegating POC testing responsibilities, frontline HCW can free up valuable time, allowing them to attend to a larger number of patients per clinic session. This redistribution of workload can optimize clinic efficiency and enhance access to essential diagnostic services. This aligns with other research studies as well as WHO recommendations which have emphasized that LHW are well placed to perform POC testing [5,10,21,23,24], compared to frontline HCW who have less availability for additional tasks. Prior research also highlights that the greatest benefits from task shifting could be more pronounced in PHC care settings [5,33] as task shifting can significantly expand access to timely diagnostics and reduce unnecessary referrals of patients or samples to higher-level health facilities. This could save the patient time and cost as well as potentially contribute to improving global health milestones, as echoed by other studies [25,31,34]. In many settings, there are existing lay cadres whose scope could be broadened/re-modelled to include task shifted testing for POC tests [5,10]. With decreased international funding, enhancing integrated diagnostic testing efficiencies, amongst diminishing resources, is a priority for low- and middle-income countries.

In model 2, task shifted CD4 POC testing contributed to a moderately high CD4 cell count testing coverage of 86% among patients initiating ART and or with high HIV VL. This could support early identification of patients with AHD, especially as measurement of CD4 has declined to very low levels since the treat-all recommendation, more-so in sub-Saharan Africa [35].

Even though some studies have highlighted that implementation of POC tests could inevitably increase patient waiting times and or cause patients to exit care while waiting between rooms [36], for this study the POC room became an essential part of the patient flow with patients progressing through the various clinic stations (waiting room, clinician consultation, POC-room, and pharmacy). The POC room provided a defined space for POC testing, and this could improve the performance of tests within controlled environments and reduce the variability introduced by busy-complex clinical areas, which usually lack work surfaces for the array of POC tests. However, insufficient documentation of POC test result turn-around time and subsequent communication of results to clinicians in our dataset prevented us from directly commenting on this.

Effective user training and ongoing monitoring support are crucial for task shifted POCT services. For this study, the district laboratory manager supported and mentored the LHWs in the five PHCs for POCT quality, to help maintain the trueness results. The 8.3% PIMA CD4+ cell count testing error rate obtained in our study is comparable with error rates from a systematic review study that found PIMA CD4 median error rates of 8–10%, depending on the setting [37]. Such results are indicative of the acceptable quality of task shifted CD4 testing services.

The production of the PIMA CD4 instrument was discontinued in March 2022, by the manufacturer (Abbott, Jena, Germany) due to the low volumes of CD4 tests ordered [31]. This has resulted in a considerable reduction in available CD4 testing options, and access to CD4 testing has become a substantial barrier for the AHD package of care [8].

While task shifting holds great promise, it must be implemented with clarity on LHW work-roles along with POCT, otherwise it can lead to ‘task dumping’ with potential deterioration in POCT quality. To support sustainable scaling of TS for the repertoire of POC tests with LHW, especially in decentralized health facilities, national health policy and strategy reforms are needed to support formalization of task shifted multi-disease POCT. Recent reports highlight that the HDA lay cadre was phased-out in Malawi as they had no formal technical training and that the Medical Council of Malawi did not recognize or register them [38]. The report further highlights that this process was undertaken to standardize the numerous lay cadre titles originally created by various non-governmental organizations, thereby preparing for their systematic transition into government health services. Nevertheless, long-term sustainability of TS for POCT services could be assured if national laboratory policies and strategies as well as vertical disease implementation strategies emphasize the transversal role of LHW for multi-disease POCT [10]. Establishing clear guidelines on POC tests suitable for task-shifting to LHW, alongside national training programs for POCT and a framework for sustained support of delegated testing, is essential.
